title: OrbiFragsNets: Automatic Annotation of Orbitrap MS2 Spectra Using Networks
author: Chingate, Drewes, et al.
materials: The annotation of the MS2 spectra could become the first step in the data processing for identification of unknown compounds. Automatic annotation of MS2 spectra increases the confidence in the alignment of features when comparing samples, as there is already certainty on the identity of the feature, furthermore, the confidence in approaches such as molecular networking would increase, as no mass error is needed when the spectrum can be aligned directly.

steps.title: Install required Python libraries
steps.instruction: Install Python 3 and the following libraries before proceeding: Numpy, Pandas, scipy, IPython, tabulate, datetime, os, and PyOpenMS (https://pyopenms.readthedocs.io). Use pip or conda as preferred.

steps.title: Download OrbiFragsNets repository
steps.instruction: Open the GitHub repository https://github.com/EdwinChingate/OrbiFragsNets, click the “Code” button, select “Download ZIP”, and extract the archive to a folder of your choice.

steps.title: Verify notebook and folder structure
steps.instruction: Confirm that the extracted folder contains the notebook file OrbiFragsNets_Notebook.ipynb and the subfolders ‘Data’, ‘Functions’, and ‘Parameters’.

steps.title: Obtain and convert raw data
steps.instruction: Copy your raw instrument files (extension .raw) to the analysis computer. Convert each file to .mzML format with ProteoWizard msConvert, keeping profile mode and avoiding filters. Example command in a Linux terminal: msconvert "$file" –mzML.

steps.title: Place mzML files in Data folder
steps.instruction: Move all resulting .mzML files into the ‘Data’ subfolder inside the OrbiFragsNets working directory.

steps.title: Charge libraries
steps.instruction: Execute the notebook cell labeled “Charge libraries” to load required functions and reference libraries.

steps.title: Charge your data file
steps.instruction: In the cell “Charge your data file”, assign the name of the .mzML file you wish to analyse to the string variable ‘DataSetName’, then run the function ChargeDataSet. The loaded spectrum will be stored in the variable DataSet.

steps.title: Edit maximum atomic subscripts
steps.instruction: Open Parameters/MaxAtomicSubscripts.csv with a text editor (e.g., gedit) or spreadsheet software. Set the maximum number of atoms you expect for each element; you may use high values (>50) at the cost of longer execution time in the MoleculesCand function.

steps.title: Edit analysis parameters
steps.instruction: Open Parameters/ParametersTable.csv similarly and adjust desired parameters. Pay particular attention to NoiseTresInt, which strongly influences execution time in the NumpyMSPeaksIdentification function. The repository manual provides full descriptions of each parameter.

steps.title: Define target m/z and run annotation
steps.instruction: Set the target molecule m/z as the protonated adduct (+H+) in the notebook and execute the function OrbiFragsNets. For anionic analysis, change the ‘ionization’ entry in ParametersTable.csv from ‘+’ to ‘-’ before running the function.

steps.title: Visualize results table
steps.instruction: Run the notebook cell named “ShowDF” to display the results DataFrame containing predicted m/z, measured m/z, confidence intervals, relative intensities, and molecular formulas.

steps.title: Export results
steps.instruction: In the cell “Export results”, export the displayed table as an .xlsx or .csv file. The exported columns include ‘Predicted m/z (Da)’, ‘Relative intensity (%)’, and ‘Molecular formula’, which can be used for downstream searches (e.g., MSBank).

steps.title: Assign 10 ppm confidence for comparison
steps.instruction: When comparing pre‑processed, centroided data, manually set the confidence interval to 10 ppm in both OrbiFragsNets and SIRIUS (the notebook ‘OrbiFragsNets_example.ipynb’ contains a script for this).
